summary: Defines a set of RADIUS attributes to support compulsory tunneling in dial-up networks, such as which tunnel type and where it ends. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2868 defines fields that a RADIUS server can use to tell network equipment how to set up a compulsory tunnel. The fields can describe the tunnel type, its endpoints, and other settings. The RFC also warns that the password protection does not hide tunnel passwords from every server along the way.

subtitle: How a RADIUS server describes a tunnel and its endpoints to network equipment.

tldr.problem: Compulsory tunneling creates a tunnel without the user's choice, so tunnel endpoints need a standard way to receive its configuration.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2868 defines RADIUS attributes for tunnel type, medium, endpoints, credentials, grouping, assignment, preference, and authentication names. Tags associate attributes with a tunnel.
tldr.outcome: The Informational RFC updates RFC 2865 and is itself updated by RFC 3575. Its password protection does not hide the password from RADIUS proxies.

today: RFC 2868 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 2865. It is itself updated by RFC 3575 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Tunnel Attributes Are Needed
sections.content:
Some tunnels are voluntary: a user asks to create one for a particular purpose. In compulsory tunneling, the tunnel is created without the user's action or choice. A RADIUS server therefore needs to send tunnel information to the tunnel endpoints.

RFC 2868 defines attributes for carrying that information in RADIUS packets. The RFC points to RFC 2809 for recommendations and examples of applying these attributes to L2TP.
sections.plainLanguage: When a network creates a tunnel for a user, the equipment at each end needs the same setup details. These RADIUS fields carry those details from the server.

sections.title: Tags and Alternative Tunnels
sections.content:
A RADIUS packet may contain multiple instances of an attribute. Attributes for one tunnel SHOULD use the same Tag value so the recipient can group them. Valid tags run from 0x01 through 0x1F; a tag that is not used MUST be zero for fixed-size attributes.

When a server returns several tunnel descriptions, the initiator SHOULD treat them as alternatives. A Tunnel-Preference attribute ranks each alternative: the numerically lowest value is preferred. Equal values leave the choice to local metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: A tag lets the receiver group fields that describe the same tunnel. If the server offers alternatives, a preference value shows which one to try first.

sections.title: The Tunnel Attributes
sections.content:
The RFC defines ten attributes. Tunnel-Type identifies the protocol; Tunnel-Medium-Type identifies the transport medium. Tunnel-Client-Endpoint and Tunnel-Server-Endpoint identify the two ends. Tunnel-Password carries a password, while Tunnel-Private-Group-ID identifies a private group and Tunnel-Assignment-ID selects a tunnel for a session.

Tunnel-Preference ranks alternatives. Tunnel-Client-Auth-ID and Tunnel-Server-Auth-ID carry the names used by each endpoint during tunnel authentication. If an initiator receives only unknown or unsupported tunnel types, it MUST behave as if it received an Access-Reject. Sessions without an assignment ID use an unnamed tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: The fields describe the kind of tunnel, its two endpoints, and any password or group assignment. Other fields rank alternatives and provide the authentication names used at each end.

sections.title: How Tunnel-Password Is Encoded
sections.content:
Tunnel-Password is allowed only in an Access-Accept packet. It includes a two-octet Salt whose most significant bit MUST be set and whose value MUST be unique within that packet. The encrypted string begins with a one-octet data length and includes the password and, when needed, padding to a multiple of 16 octets.

The RFC describes encryption in 16-octet blocks using MD5-based values derived from the RADIUS shared secret, the Request Authenticator, the salt, and the previous ciphertext block. A receiver reverses those steps to recover the string.
sections.plainLanguage: The password field uses a salt and a shared secret to encode the password in blocks. This is only protection within the RADIUS exchange; an intervening RADIUS proxy can still read the password.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RADIUS proxies can learn Tunnel-Password contents because of how the attribute is protected. The RFC says the attribute SHOULD NOT be sent through relatively untrusted proxies, and SHOULD NOT be returned to a client unless its request had a verified Signature Attribute.

Tunnel security applies only between tunnel endpoints in the compulsory-tunneling case. End users SHOULD NOT rely on it to protect their data, and tunnel encryption MUST NOT replace end-to-end security.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS proxies may see the tunnel password. Also, tunnel protection covers only the connection between the tunnel endpoints, so it does not replace protection between the user's own applications.

sections.title: Assigned Attribute Values
sections.content: The RFC defines values 1 through 12 for Tunnel-Type and values 1 through 15 for Tunnel-Medium-Type. Other values in both lists are available for assignment by IANA under IETF Consensus.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC assigns the initial numbers for tunnel types and media. IANA can assign other values when the IETF reaches consensus.

fields.name: Tag
fields.desc: Groups attributes for one tunnel; zero means unused.
